philology.title: Where each word "lives"
philology.caption: Three words describe the unseen realm below. Gehenna is different: a real valley you can walk through in Jerusalem today. Tap a layer.

hotspots.label: Gehenna
hotspots.text: Greek form of the Hebrew Gey Hinnom, the Valley of Hinnom beside Jerusalem. A real place of shame and burning, used by Jesus as a metaphor.

hotspots.label: Sheol
hotspots.text: Hebrew word for the realm of the dead, often translated "the grave" or "the pit" (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not associated with punishment or reward.

hotspots.label: Hades
hotspots.text: Greek equivalent of Sheol. The Septuagint uses Hades to translate Sheol. A temporary holding place for the dead, not a place of torment or bliss.

hotspots.label: Tartarus
hotspots.text: Used in 2 Peter 2:4: the angels that sinned were cast into tartarus, "into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment".

svg_labels.Hebrew · the grave, realm of all the dea: Hebrew · the grave, realm of all the dead
svg_labels.Greek name for the same realm: Greek name for the same realm

gehenna.title: Jerusalem and the Valley of Hinnom
gehenna.caption: Schematic map, not to scale. Gehenna was a real valley outside the city walls, once a site of child sacrifice. Its later link with a burning city dump is debated by scholars (see Straw Men and Quick Replies).

hotspots.label: Valley of Hinnom
hotspots.text: Gey Hinnom, "Gehenna". Site of Topheth, where children were sacrificed by fire (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 19:6). A symbol of shame and judgment.

hotspots.label: Kidron Valley
hotspots.text: The Kidron Valley encompasses the Valley of Hinnom. An Early Roman (1st century CE) city dump has been excavated in the Kidron area.

hotspots.label: Temple Mount
hotspots.text: The heart of the city. Gehenna lay just outside its walls, within sight of the people Jesus addressed.

hotspots.label: Mount of Olives
hotspots.text: Across the Kidron Valley to the east.

early.title: The six early schools of theology
early.caption: In the first centuries, the major teaching centres disagreed about hell. Only one taught eternal conscious torment. Tap a city.

hotspots.label: Alexandria (2nd c.)
hotspots.text: Taught that punishment is temporary and purifying, ending in restoration.

hotspots.label: Antioch (3rd c.)
hotspots.text: Literal, historical reading of Scripture; also taught restoration.

hotspots.label: Caesarea (3rd c.)
hotspots.text: Influenced by Origen; taught restoration.

hotspots.label: Eastern Syria (4th c.)
hotspots.text: Syriac tradition: divine punishment is temporary and aimed at correction.

hotspots.label: Asia Minor (3rd c.)
hotspots.text: Taught annihilationism: the wicked are ultimately destroyed, not tormented forever.

hotspots.label: Hippo (late 4th–5th c.)
hotspots.text: Augustine’s school in North Africa: the only one that taught eternal conscious torment.

lakeoffire.title: A lake of "fire and sulfur" you can visit
lakeoffire.caption: The Dead Sea: the lowest point on earth, rich in sulfur, visited for healing. Fire and sulfur were also used to refine gold. The book reads the lake of fire as purification.

hotspots.label: Dead Sea
hotspots.text: The lowest point on Earth’s surface. Its mineral-rich waters, with sulfur, are known for healing and purifying; bathing there can feel like dipping in fire.

hotspots.label: Sodom & Gomorrah
hotspots.text: The Lord rained "sulfur and fire" on them (Genesis 19:24). Yet Ezekiel 16:53-55 promises God will restore the fortunes of Sodom.

hotspots.label: Jordan River
hotspots.text: Flows south from the Sea of Galilee into the Dead Sea.

hotspots.label: Jerusalem
hotspots.text: West of the Dead Sea, in the hills of Judea.

unquenchable.title: The refiner’s fire
unquenchable.caption: In Scripture, fire often purifies: metal is heated until the dross rises and is removed. "He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver" (Malachi 3:3).

hotspots.label: Dross
hotspots.text: Impurities rise to the surface and are skimmed away: the sin is destroyed, not the person.

hotspots.label: Pure silver
hotspots.text: What remains after refining. Fire tests and cleanses; it does not exist to torture.

hotspots.label: The fire
hotspots.text: Unquenchable fire "will not stop until it fully completes its task". It burns what it is meant to burn.

torah.title: What the Torah says happens at death
torah.caption: In the Torah, the dead "go down to Sheol", the realm of the dead. In Judaism, Sheol is where all souls rest until judgment day, not a place of torment.

hotspots.label: Sheol
hotspots.text: Jacob said, "I shall go down to Sheol to my son, mourning" (Genesis 37:34-35). Sheol simply means the realm of the dead, like a grave.

hotspots.label: Blessings and curses
hotspots.text: The Torah’s blessings are earthly: barns, flocks, the land (Deuteronomy 28). Its penalties, too, concern this life.

lazarus.title: The great chasm in the parable
lazarus.caption: A parable for a Jewish audience, full of symbolic names and images. It is read as a story with a message, not a literal map of the afterlife.

hotspots.label: Abraham’s side
hotspots.text: Lazarus, the poor man, is comforted. His Hebrew name, Eleazar, means "God’s Help" and recalls Abraham’s steward Eleazar (Genesis 15:2-3).

hotspots.label: The great chasm
hotspots.text: A fixed gulf separates the two. The parable reverses their fortunes in life.

hotspots.label: The rich man in Hades
hotspots.text: He is in BASANOS: usually translated "torment", but the word means a touchstone, a test.

narrow.title: Two roads, two gates
narrow.caption: The two-paths image is a familiar Jewish theme (Deuteronomy 30:19; Psalm 1:6): God’s way leads to blessing in life, the way of wickedness to destructive consequences.

hotspots.label: Narrow gate
hotspots.text: "Small is the gate and narrow the road that leads to life, and only a few find it" (Matthew 7:14).

hotspots.label: Wide gate
hotspots.text: "Wide is the gate and broad is the road that leads to destruction" (Matthew 7:13).

sheepgoats.title: Sheep and goats: judging the nations
sheepgoats.caption: The nations are judged by how they treated "the least of these" (Matthew 25:40). The Greek word for punishment, kolasis, carried the sense of correction.

hotspots.label: Sheep
hotspots.text: Those who fed the hungry, welcomed strangers, clothed the naked and visited the sick and imprisoned.

hotspots.label: Goats
hotspots.text: Those who failed to care for the least. Their punishment is kolasis, a word originally used for corrective, remedial punishment.

wheattares.title: Wheat and darnel: hard to tell apart
wheattares.caption: Darnel (Greek zizania) looks almost exactly like wheat while it grows. The difference shows when the ears form, which is why the farmer says to let both grow until the harvest (Matthew 13:29-30).

hotspots.label: Wheat
hotspots.text: The good seed: the "children of the kingdom" (Matthew 13:38). Its full ears appear at harvest.

hotspots.label: Darnel
hotspots.text: A weed that mimics wheat in the field. Its grain is harmful to eat, so it was separated out at harvest and burned.

hotspots.label: The harvest
hotspots.text: Jesus calls it "the end of the age" (Matthew 13:39-40). Readers differ on whether this is the close of the old-covenant age or the end of history.
